title: Computer-use models will agentify the web, not APIs — Dhruv Batra, Yutori

summary:
Batra argues that AI agents will drive most web activity, but rejects the claim that the web will meet them via APIs. APIs may exist at the head of the distribution, but not across the long tail, which includes roughly 200 million active sites whose infrastructure changes over decades. He illustrates this with restaurant menus in three modes: easy text, a PDF, and a gallery of JPEG images that must be OCR'd, and with school-district procurement sites that culminate in a district requiring FOIA requests and returning scanned PDFs on Google Drive.

Even when APIs are absent, reading HTML does not rescue the agent: an NBA score arrives via async JSON rather than the initial HTML, and a product page signals 'sold out' via a zero quantity rendered as a grayed, unclickable option. State is calculated and rendered, making the browser closer to a game engine than a document and pixels the source of truth. This is the bitter lesson: per-site scaffolds do not generalize, so vision is the general solution.

Yutori's Navigator takes screenshots in and clicks out like a human, can write JavaScript when it is faster than clicking, and verifies its own work by re-reading pixels. Multiple Navigators can run in parallel cloud sandboxes, giving superhuman parallelism. On a popular Mind2Web-style benchmark, Navigator N1.5 sits at 97% human eval, failing 8 of 300 trajectories, and Batra argues the benchmark should be retired. Cost per 20-30 step task is roughly $0.80 versus about $2.30 for frontier models, and tasks sometimes complete in under 100 milliseconds. Batra concludes that the messy stack of bots clicking in browsers will itself become the de facto API, with a higher-level endpoint delivering structured results under a penny.

sections.title: The argument, and the part of it that is wrong
sections.summary: Batra frames the popular narrative that agents will dominate the web and meet it through APIs and protocols like MCP. He accepts the agent premise but calls the API premise delusional, especially for the long tail.

sections.title: Restaurant menus on easy, medium, and hard mode
sections.summary: He walks through three restaurant websites: plain text with prices, a menu hidden behind a PDF, and a gallery of JPEG images that require OCR, showing why a gluten-free menu endpoint will not exist.

sections.title: School district procurement, up to a FOIA request
sections.summary: Using the example of selling laptops to roughly 15,000 to 20,000 US school districts, he shows procurement sites that range from portals to scanned PDFs to a district that requires FOIA requests, scans the requester's email, uploads it to Google Drive, and attaches PDFs.

sections.title: 200 million active sites that change slowly
sections.summary: Batra emphasizes the massive long tail of about 200 million active sites whose infrastructure, including fax use, changes over decades, so agents cannot expect APIs to appear.

sections.title: Why reading the HTML does not rescue it
sections.summary: He shows that an NBA score is not in the initial HTML but arrives later via an async JSON call, and that stock status is encoded as a zero quantity rendered as a grayed option, not as text.

sections.title: Sold out is not text, it is a rendered zero
sections.summary: He elaborates that on a product page the dropdown never says 'sold out' or 'available'; a backend quantity of zero triggers a script that grays out and disables the option, meaning the screen-rendered state is computed.

sections.title: The browser is a rendering engine, pixels are the truth
sections.summary: Batra argues the browser is closer to a game engine than a document, so pixels are the source of truth, making vision the only general approach. He calls this the bitter lesson for web agents.

sections.title: Navigator, and writing JavaScript when that is faster
sections.summary: He introduces Yutori's Navigator, first released the previous November, which screenshots in and clicks out like a human, demonstrates a 20-40 step discount-code verification task, then shows the newer model writing a small JavaScript function to fill multiple form fields at once via a Chrome extension, treating the browser as both a rendering engine and a code-execution engine with the screenshot as ground truth.

sections.title: Parallel orchestrators and superhuman button-clicking
sections.summary: Batra notes that orchestrators can launch many Navigator instances in parallel cloud sandboxes, each clicking through different websites, achieving parallelism no single human could match.

sections.title: Are computer use models actually good enough
sections.summary: He pushes back on the perception that computer-use progress is slow, showing a benchmark plot where Navigator N1.5 hits 97% human eval, failing only 8 of 300 trajectories on 30-50 step tasks, and argues such saturated benchmarks should be retired in favor of harder ones.

sections.title: Latency and cost per task
sections.summary: He compares Navigator N1.5 to frontier models like Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 on browser-use benchmarks, noting comparable accuracy but emphasizing that the smaller-footprint Navigator is faster and cheaper: roughly $0.80 versus $2.30 per 20-30 step task, enabling scale.

sections.title: Another layer of mess that we will call an API
sections.summary: Batra concludes by rejecting the fantasy that 30 years of human-facing infrastructure will be reinvented in 5-10 years, then predicts that accuracy will keep rising while latency and cost keep falling. Hundreds of bots will click in browsers in the background, return structured results in under 100 milliseconds for under a penny, and users will simply call that an API.

evidence.supports: Batra explicitly rejects the 'web will provide APIs' claim while accepting that agents will dominate actions on the web.
